title: ViewModel & State Holders
scopeHtml: Scope: ViewModel internals, scoping, SavedStateHandle, factories, plain state holders, Android-type hygiene, init/lazy work, leaks and ViewModel testing. Flow/coroutine mechanics live in A1, Compose state in A3, event delivery in chunk 03.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does ViewModel solve, and exactly what does it survive and not survive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who say "it survives rotation" and stop have never been bitten by process death. This is the baseline signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ViewModel is a screen-scoped holder for UI state and the work that produces it. It lives in a ViewModelStore owned by an Activity, Fragment or NavBackStackEntry, so it survives configuration changes like rotation, dark-mode toggle or locale change. It does not survive process death, and it does not survive the user finishing the screen (back press, finish()), because then the owner clears the store and calls onCleared().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Before ViewModel, the Activity was destroyed and recreated on a configuration change, so in-memory state and in-flight requests were lost. ViewModel moves state out of the recreated object into a holder the framework retains across that recreation.

Event                          ViewModel alive?   Why
-----------------------------  -----------------  ------------------------------------
Rotation / font scale / locale yes                store retained across recreation
Back press / finish()          no (onCleared)     owner is really going away
Fragment replaced, popped      no (onCleared)     FragmentManager clears child store
Nav entry popped               no (onCleared)     NavBackStackEntry cleared
App in background, OS kills    no (process gone)  nothing in memory survives
User swipes app from recents   no                 task and saved state both gone

Rule of thumb: ViewModel = "same process, same screen instance, new view". Anything that must outlive the process goes to SavedStateHandle (small, transient) or disk (Room/DataStore).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProfileUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<ProfileUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
        _state.update { it.copy(loading = false, profile = repo.load()) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "ViewModel survives process death". It does not.
  • Treating ViewModel as a cache for data that is expensive to rebuild; after a process kill it is rebuilt from scratch.
  • Believing rotation never kills in-flight work: viewModelScope work continues, but only because the scope is tied to the ViewModel, not the Activity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does onCleared run on rotation? → No, only when the owner is permanently finished.
  2. Does ViewModel survive Activity recreation from "Don't keep activities"? → That simulates destroy with isChangingConfigurations=false, so the store is cleared. Use it to test finish-like behavior, not rotation.
  3. How do you survive process death? → SavedStateHandle for IDs and inputs, disk for data, and rebuild the rest from the data layer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "holds data across rotation". Senior: names the owner/store mechanism, the three lifetimes (config change, finish, process death), and designs the VM to rebuild from minimal saved state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen kept a selected address only in the ViewModel. Backgrounded for 20 minutes on a 3 GB device, the process died and users came back to an empty form; the fix was storing the address ID in SavedStateHandle.

questions.promptHtml: Compare onSaveInstanceState, ViewModel, SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable. When do you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand the state-retention layers rather than pattern-matching.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ViewModel retains arbitrary objects across config change but not process death. onSaveInstanceState and SavedStateHandle write a Bundle that survives system-initiated process death, but only for small, parcelable data. SavedStateHandle is the ViewModel-friendly wrapper over the same Bundle. rememberSaveable is the Compose equivalent for UI-element state. Persistent data goes to disk.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism           Survives config change  Survives process death  Size/type limit        Use for
------------------  ----------------------  ----------------------  ---------------------  ---------------------------
remember            no                      no                      none                   transient UI state
rememberSaveable    yes                     yes (Bundle)            Bundle types / Saver   scroll, text field, toggles
ViewModel field     yes                     no                      none                   screen state, in-flight work
SavedStateHandle    yes                     yes (Bundle)            small, ~tens of KB     IDs, query, selected tab
Room/DataStore      yes                     yes (disk)              disk                   real data, drafts

Official guidance: state used in business logic lives in the ViewModel and is saved via SavedStateHandle; state used in UI logic uses rememberSaveable. None of these survive the user swiping the app away or force stop: saved state is tied to the task stack.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SearchViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: SearchRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val query: StateFlow<String> = handle.getStateFlow("query", "")
    val results = query.debounce(300).flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
    fun onQuery(q: String) { handle["query"] = q }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a 2 MB list in SavedStateHandle; the Bundle goes through Binder and can throw TransactionTooLargeException.
  • Saving the data instead of the key to re-fetch it.
  • Assuming saved state is restored after the user closed the app from recents.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why save an ID rather than the object? → Small, stable, avoids stale data; rebuild from the repository.
  2. How do you test process death? → adb shell am kill <pkg> after backgrounding, or Developer Options "Don't keep activities" for the Activity-destroy path.
  3. What if state must survive the user closing the app? → Persist drafts to disk explicitly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE picks ViewModel for everything. Senior assigns each piece of state to a retention tier and explicitly lists what is lost in each failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen lost its query after OS kills (3% of sessions on low-RAM devices) until the query moved into SavedStateHandle.

questions.promptHtml: What is viewModelScope, what dispatcher does it use, and what happens to its coroutines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know where work should run and when it stops.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: viewModelScope is a CoroutineScope owned by the ViewModel. It uses a SupervisorJob plus Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so a failing child does not cancel siblings, and code starts on the main thread. When the ViewModel is cleared the scope is cancelled, which cancels all running coroutines.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Lifecycle: created lazily on first access, stored in the ViewModel's closeable map, closed during clear(). Cancellation is cooperative: a blocking call with no suspension point keeps running.
  • Main.immediate means that if you call launch from the main thread, the body runs synchronously until its first suspension. This is why init { viewModelScope.launch { ... } } can touch state before the constructor finishes if you are not careful with field initialization order.
  • SupervisorJob: an uncaught exception in one launch goes to the thread's uncaught handler (crash) unless you add a CoroutineExceptionHandler or try/catch; it does not cancel other launches.
  • Work that must outlive the screen (upload, payment confirmation) does not belong here; use WorkManager or an application-scoped scope (see A1/A5).
  • Lifecycle 2.9 docs also show passing a custom CoroutineScope to the ViewModel constructor for testing or a different dispatcher (verify the exact API for your lifecycle version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedViewModel(private val repo: FeedRepo) : ViewModel() {
    fun load() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val items = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { repo.parseHeavy() } // off main
            _items.value = items // back on Main.immediate
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing blocking IO directly in launch, freezing the main thread.
  • Expecting an exception in launch to be catchable by try/catch around the launch call.
  • Using viewModelScope for work that must complete after the user leaves.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why SupervisorJob? → One failed child (say analytics) must not cancel the screen's other work.
  2. What does cancel do to a blocking loop? → Nothing until it checks isActive or suspends.
  3. How do you test code on Main.immediate? → Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher); see the testing question.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "scope tied to ViewModel, cancelled on clear". Senior adds dispatcher, supervisor semantics, exception routing and the limit on what work may live there.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A draft-save in viewModelScope was cancelled when the user pressed back, losing 1 in 200 drafts; moving it to a WorkManager job fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does a ViewModel actually survive a configuration change? Walk me through ViewModelProvider, ViewModelStore and the owner.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use ViewModel from people who understand it, which matters when debugging scoping bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ViewModelStoreOwner (ComponentActivity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry) exposes a ViewModelStore, essentially a map from string key to ViewModel. ViewModelProvider(owner, factory).get(Class) looks up the key and only calls the factory on a miss. On a config change the Activity hands its store to the new instance through the non-configuration instance mechanism. On a real finish, a lifecycle observer calls store.clear(), which calls each ViewModel's onCleared.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity A1 --onRetainNonConfigurationInstance--> NonConfigurationInstances{ viewModelStore }
   | destroyed (rotation)                                  |
   v                                                       v
Activity A2 created --getViewModelStore()--> reuses same store -> same ViewModel instance

Real finish: ON_DESTROY observed && !isChangingConfigurations -> viewModelStore.clear()
  • Key: default is "androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelProvider.DefaultKey:" plus the class canonical name. Two lookups of the same class in the same store return the same instance; pass an explicit key to hold several instances of one class (e.g. per item ID).
  • Fragments: the FragmentManager keeps a FragmentManagerViewModel (itself retained) holding child stores, which is why fragment VMs survive recreation.
  • Navigation: NavController keeps a NavControllerViewModel mapping each back stack entry to its own store, so a ViewModel lives while the entry is on the back stack and is cleared when popped.
  • Because the factory is only consulted on a miss, a changed factory dependency after the first creation is ignored. This explains "my new argument isn't applied" bugs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Same store + same key => same instance
val a = ViewModelProvider(this)[CartViewModel::class.java]
val b = ViewModelProvider(this)[CartViewModel::class.java]
check(a === b)

// Distinct instances per key in one store
val vmA = ViewModelProvider(this)["item-1", ItemViewModel::class.java]
val vmB = ViewModelProvider(this)["item-2", ItemViewModel::class.java]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the Activity holds the ViewModel directly; it holds the store.
  • Passing different arguments on re-entry and expecting a new ViewModel.
  • Assuming a retained store means the ViewModel is immune to process death.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not hold the ViewModel in a static map? → No lifecycle-driven clear; leaks and cross-instance bleed.
  2. What happens to the store when Activity A is replaced by Activity B? → Separate owners, separate stores.
  3. How does a nav-scoped VM get cleared when the entry is popped? → NavControllerViewModel.clearBackStackEntry drops its store, which clears.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "the framework retains it". Senior explains owner, store, key and the cleared-vs-recreated branch, and uses that to explain scoping bugs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A list of per-item ViewModels used the default key, so every row shared one instance and showed the first item's data until a key was added.

questions.promptHtml: How do you create a ViewModel that needs constructor dependencies without Hilt? Explain ViewModelProvider.Factory and CreationExtras.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Manual DI and understanding what Hilt generates under the hood.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The framework instantiates ViewModels, so you provide a ViewModelProvider.Factory. Modern way: override create(Class, CreationExtras), or use the viewModelFactory { initializer { ... } } DSL. CreationExtras is a typed map that carries the Application (APPLICATION_KEY), the default args and the SavedStateRegistry owner, from which createSavedStateHandle() builds the handle. A no-arg or SavedStateHandle-only ViewModel needs no custom factory.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The older create(Class) variant cannot reach the owner, so SavedStateHandle required an AbstractSavedStateViewModelFactory. CreationExtras (Lifecycle 2.5+) replaced that plumbing.
  • Custom keys: define CreationExtras.Key<T>() and pass extras into viewModel(factory, extras) for dependencies the Application cannot provide (also useful in KMP modules without Android types).
  • Each initializer is keyed by the ViewModel class; the DSL throws if you request a class you did not register.
  • Hilt generates this factory for @HiltViewModel classes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DetailViewModel(
    private val repo: DetailRepo,
    private val handle: SavedStateHandle,
) : ViewModel() {
    companion object {
        val Factory: ViewModelProvider.Factory = viewModelFactory {
            initializer {
                val app = this[ViewModelProvider.AndroidViewModelFactory.APPLICATION_KEY] as MyApp
                DetailViewModel(app.detailRepo, createSavedStateHandle())
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun DetailRoute(vm: DetailViewModel = viewModel(factory = DetailViewModel.Factory)) { /* ... */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Capturing an Activity or Context in the factory lambda, so the retained ViewModel holds a destroyed Activity.
  • Constructing the ViewModel with DetailViewModel(...) directly in a composable: it is then not in any store and dies on recreation.
  • A new factory instance with different arguments is ignored if the store already has the ViewModel.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does SavedStateHandle come from in the factory? → CreationExtras.createSavedStateHandle().
  2. How do you pass a runtime ID? → Via nav arguments in the handle, or a custom extras key, or assisted injection with Hilt.
  3. Why prefer the DSL? → Type-safe, avoids unchecked casts and manual class checks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes a Factory with a when on modelClass. Senior uses extras, knows why create(Class) is legacy, and knows the factory is consulted only on store misses.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-written factory captured the Activity as Context; LeakCanary flagged it after every rotation until the Application context was used.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (800k DAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM or less) shows a memory growth trend: after 10 rotations on the article screen, LeakCanary reports a retained ArticleActivity (about 18 MB with its bitmaps). Crash rate for OOM is 0.6%. This is the ViewModel:

class ArticleViewModel(
    private val activity: ArticleActivity,
    private val repo: ArticleRepo,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val _title = MutableLiveData<String>()
    val title: LiveData<String> = _title

    fun load(id: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val a = repo.get(id)
            _title.value = a.title
            activity.supportActionBar?.title = a.title
        }
    }
}

It is created in onCreate with a custom factory that passes this.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and what is your fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WeakReference to the activity". That hides the lifetime bug, still lets the ViewModel do UI work, and breaks when the weak ref clears mid-coroutine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the factory the only creation path? Are there other retained objects (singletons, listeners) also referencing the Activity? Is the leak present on every rotation or only the second one? Does the screen use Fragments? These separate a single leak path from several.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that stops passing the Activity: have the ViewModel expose the title and let the Activity set the action bar. Small, low-risk diff.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ViewModel holds Activity strongly (obvious from code); (b) a LiveData observer or callback registered in the ViewModel referencing the Activity; (c) a static singleton also referencing it; (d) the Activity itself was fine and the bitmap cache is the growth (red herring if the heap dump shows ViewModel on the path).
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace: GC Root: ... ViewModelStore -> ArticleViewModel.activity -> ArticleActivity. Android Studio heap dump, filter on ArticleActivity, count instances after 10 rotations (expected 1, observed 11). Static analysis: grep for Context/Activity/View/Fragment types in ViewModel constructors and fields; a lint rule or Konsist test enforces it.
  5. Root cause: The ViewModel outlives the Activity by design (retained across config change). A strong field to the first Activity pins that instance and its whole view tree. After rotation the ViewModel still points at the dead one, so UI writes also go to a destroyed Activity.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove the constructor parameter; the Activity observes title and sets the action bar. Long-term: if a Context is truly needed use the Application context via APPLICATION_KEY, or inject an abstraction (e.g. a string provider) and keep UI in the UI layer.
class ArticleViewModel(private val repo: ArticleRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _title = MutableStateFlow("")
    val title: StateFlow<String> = _title.asStateFlow()
    fun load(id: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _title.value = repo.get(id).title }
}
  1. Prevention: Konsist/lint rule banning Activity/Fragment/View/Context types in ViewModel classes; LeakCanary in debug and a rotation test in CI; code review checklist.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use WeakReference (masks the design flaw), and I would not make the ViewModel AndroidViewModel just to dodge the constructor issue if Context is only used for strings.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if you need a string resource in the ViewModel? → Emit a resource ID or a UiText wrapper and resolve it in the UI.
  • Is AndroidViewModel safe? → Yes for Application context, but it hampers pure-JVM tests; prefer injecting an abstraction.
  • Would a Fragment reference be different? → Same problem; Fragment views are even heavier.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team fixed three "random" OOMs by deleting an image cache, then found the real cause two releases later: a ViewModel held a callback lambda capturing the Activity, which a single heap-dump query would have shown.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests WeakReference or does not know why a retained object pins the Activity.
  • Hire: identifies the retained-ViewModel/Activity lifetime mismatch, fixes with state exposure, names LeakCanary.
  • Strong hire: adds an automated architecture check, discusses Application-context alternatives and why UI calls belong in the UI.

questions.promptHtml: What are the practical patterns for using SavedStateHandle in a ViewModel, and what should and should not go in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you can design for process death without bloating the Bundle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I treat SavedStateHandle as the ViewModel's tiny persistent inputs: IDs, search query, selected tab, in-progress form text. I read them as flows with getStateFlow, write via set or a delegate, and rebuild everything else from the repository. I never put lists, bitmaps or domain objects in it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Backing: a key-value map persisted as a Bundle through the SavedStateRegistry. Allowed types are Bundle types, Parcelable, Serializable; custom objects need @Parcelize, a setSavedStateProvider, or the saved/saveable delegates (kotlinx.serialization saved and Compose saveable are in recent Lifecycle versions; getMutableStateFlow arrived in Lifecycle 2.9.0, verify your version).
  • Timing: the Bundle is written when the host Activity stops (onSaveInstanceState), not on every set. In Compose the official doc warns writes made after the Activity is stopped are not saved until the next onStart/onStop cycle. So a value updated by a background coroutine after the app is backgrounded may be lost.
  • Navigation arguments also arrive in the handle: with Navigation 2.8 type-safe routes use handle.toRoute<Route>().
  • Restoration: after process death the Activity restarts, a new ViewModel is created, and the handle contains the old map.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class OrdersViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val handle: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repo: OrdersRepo,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val filter = handle.getStateFlow("filter", OrderFilter.ALL.name)

    val orders: StateFlow<List<Order>> = filter
        .flatMapLatest { repo.observe(OrderFilter.valueOf(it)) }   // data rebuilt, not saved
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

    fun setFilter(f: OrderFilter) { handle["filter"] = f.name }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving the whole UiState including lists.
  • Storing a non-Parcelable class and crashing at save time (runtime IllegalArgumentException).
  • Initializing state from the handle once and then forgetting to write updates back.
  • Using the handle for data that must survive the user closing the app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. getStateFlow vs get()? → getStateFlow emits on later sets and fits flow pipelines; get() is a snapshot.
  2. How do you store an enum? → Store its name or ordinal (primitive), not the enum if you want version safety.
  3. What happens if the saved class changes between app versions? → Restoring after an update can throw; keep saved types primitive and stable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows handle["key"]. Senior defines a minimal-state rule, knows the write timing, and tests restoration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A release changed a Parcelable's fields and crashed with ClassCastException on restore for users updating mid-session; storing primitives removed the risk.

questions.promptHtml: How do viewModel() and hiltViewModel() work in Compose, and what scope does the ViewModel get?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everyone uses these helpers; few know what they bind to.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both read the nearest LocalViewModelStoreOwner and ask for a ViewModel with a default key. Inside a NavHost destination that owner is the NavBackStackEntry, so the ViewModel lives while that entry is on the back stack. Outside a NavHost it is the Activity. viewModel() uses a default factory (no-arg or SavedStateHandle only); hiltViewModel() uses the Hilt-generated factory and needs @HiltViewModel.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• viewModel() is from lifecycle-viewmodel-compose; hiltViewModel() from androidx.hilt:hilt-navigation-compose. Check the current artifact versions for your Compose BOM (verify).
  • Calling it again in a recomposition returns the same instance because the store returns the cached one.
  • Where you call matters: a call inside a child composable of a destination gets the same entry-scoped VM. A call in a non-destination dialog or bottom sheet gets the nearest owner.
  • Pass state and lambdas down, not the ViewModel: official guidance says passing it down couples composables and breaks previews.
  • For a VM tied to a parent graph: hiltViewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry(route)) (or <Route> in type-safe nav).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun OrdersRoute(onOpen: (String) -> Unit, vm: OrdersViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    OrdersScreen(state, onOpen = onOpen, onFilter = vm::setFilter) // stateless UI
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling viewModel() in a leaf composable, creating hidden coupling.
  • Using the Activity as owner for per-screen VMs, so they never clear.
  • Expecting different instances without a key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do two destinations share a VM? → Resolve it from a common parent back stack entry or an Activity-level owner.
  2. What clears the VM in a NavHost? → The entry being popped.
  3. Why not hoist the VM into every composable? → Previews and tests need only state and lambdas.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "call hiltViewModel() in the screen". Senior: names the owner, the entry lifetime, and keeps VM access at the route boundary only.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bottom-sheet composable called viewModel() with the Activity owner and kept stale search state across sessions of different products.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce app (2.5M DAU) has a checkout flow of 4 destinations sharing one CheckoutViewModel through hiltViewModel(parentEntry) of the checkout nested graph. Support tickets: "I cancelled, started a new order, and my old coupon and address were still applied" (about 1.2% of checkout starts). There are no crashes. Logs show CheckoutViewModel@7f3a created once at 10:02 and reused at 10:41. Navigation was: Cart -> Checkout -> back to Cart (via the system gesture) -> Checkout again. A recent change added popUpTo(cart) { saveState = true } and restoreState = true on bottom-bar navigation.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the stale state appear, and how do you fix it without breaking back navigation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the state in onCleared" or "just reset in onResume". onCleared never ran, and onResume resets would wipe state during legitimate navigation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exactly which navigation calls surround the repro? Is the nested graph kept by saveState/restoreState? Does the stale ViewModel also appear after process death? Did this start with that navigation change? Is the same ViewModel resolved at graph scope or at Activity scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an explicit CheckoutViewModel.reset() called when starting a new checkout from the Cart, behind a server flag, so support impact stops while the root cause is fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) saveState/restoreState keeps the graph's entries and their ViewModelStores alive while the bottom bar swaps tabs; (b) the graph's parent entry never popped, so the store was not cleared; (c) VM is Activity-scoped by mistake; (d) a singleton repository holds the coupon (red herring if VM address differs).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log VM identity (System.identityHashCode) and onCleared. Dump navController.currentBackStack after each step. Check whether checkout is in the saved back stack state. Use the Layout Inspector? Not useful here: instead a navigation test with TestNavHostController reproducing the sequence.
  5. Root cause: A ViewModel scoped to a graph entry is cleared only when that entry is popped without saving state. With saveState = true the entries are saved and their ViewModelStores kept, so restoring the tab reuses the same ViewModel and its old UI state.
  6. Fix: Short-term: reset state on a new checkout intent. Long-term: make the lifecycle explicit: pop the checkout graph with inclusive = true and no saveState on cancel/finish, and model a CheckoutSession created by the Cart's "Checkout" action with a fresh ID passed as a nav argument, so every start gets its own key.
navController.navigate(CheckoutGraph(sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString()))
// in destination
val vm: CheckoutViewModel = hiltViewModel(parentEntry) // key includes the entry, state keyed by sessionId
  1. Prevention: Instrumented nav test: start checkout, back out, start again, assert default state; log VM creations per session in analytics to catch reuse.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scope the VM to the Activity (worse), nor rely on onCleared (it will not run while state is saved). Resetting is a patch; session keys remove the ambiguity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if product wants the draft kept when the user returns within 10 minutes? → Persist a draft with TTL in the data layer, not in a ViewModel lifetime.
  • What happens at process death? → The saved nav state restores entries, the VM is recreated; only SavedStateHandle data returns.
  • Could a plain state holder help? → Not for state that must be shared across 4 destinations.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team debugged "state bleeding" for weeks in the analytics layer before drawing the back stack on a whiteboard and seeing the saved tab.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests resetting in onResume or lifecycle hacks.
  • Hire: explains entry-scoped store retention under saveState and fixes with explicit lifetime.
  • Strong hire: introduces session keys, a repro test and monitors VM reuse.

questions.contextHtml:
A travel app (400k DAU) has a flight search screen. After selecting filters (price, stops, airline) users background the app to check their email; 6% of them return to a blank results screen with default filters and a spinner that never ends. Crashlytics shows no crash. QA cannot reproduce on a Pixel 8 but can on a 2 GB Android Go device. The ViewModel:

class SearchViewModel(private val repo: FlightRepo) : ViewModel() {
    var filters by mutableStateOf(Filters())
        private set
    val results = MutableStateFlow<List<Flight>>(emptyList())
    init { /* nothing */ }
    fun search() = viewModelScope.launch { results.value = repo.search(filters) }
}

The screen calls search() from a button; the route also takes from and to nav args.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the ViewModel a singleton" or "save results in onSaveInstanceState". The first leaks and breaks, the second blows the Bundle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do repros correlate with low-memory devices and long background time? Does the spinner appear before or after restore? Are the nav args restored? Is anything saved at all? Does the repo cache survive?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fallback: on screen start, if there are no results and valid from/to exist, auto-run search so the screen is never a dead spinner. Ship fast.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) process death restored the Activity and nav args but filters lived only in ViewModel memory; (b) loading state restored as true but no job exists to finish it; (c) repository in-memory cache lost; (d) a slow network (red herring since low-end only repro).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with adb shell am kill com.example after backgrounding, or "Don't keep activities" for the destroy path; log VM creation and SavedStateHandle.keys(); check the restored nav args.
  5. Root cause: After process kill the ViewModel is a fresh instance with default Filters() and no in-flight search; the UI state restored from the previous instance does not exist, and nothing reruns the search.
  6. Fix: Keep filter inputs in SavedStateHandle, derive results from them reactively so restore automatically re-queries.
class SearchViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: FlightRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val route = handle.toRoute<SearchRoute>()           // Navigation 2.8+
    private val filters = handle.getMutableStateFlow("filters", Filters())  // Filters is @Serializable/Parcelable; verify API version
    val results = filters.flatMapLatest { repo.search(route.from, route.to, it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchState.Loading)
    fun setFilters(f: Filters) { filters.value = f }
}
  1. Prevention: Process-death test in CI (am kill between steps on an emulator), state-restoration checklist per screen, assert there is no state-only-in-memory for user input.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not saving results (large, stale); not persisting filters to disk unless the product wants cross-session memory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if filters are huge? → Persist to DataStore/Room and keep only a key in the handle.
  • Why only low-end? → Memory pressure kills background processes sooner; high-RAM devices hide the bug.
  • What about user swiping from recents? → Saved state is not restored; that is expected.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "fixed" blank screen came back because a coroutine wrote to the handle after onStop; the data was lost, and a re-query on restore made it irrelevant.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries to keep state in a singleton or static.
  • Hire: moves minimal inputs to SavedStateHandle and rebuilds results reactively.
  • Strong hire: also adds process-death tests, explains the write timing and sizes the saved data.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use a plain state holder class instead of a ViewModel, and how do the two compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you know ViewModel is not the answer to every state question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ViewModel is for state tied to a destination that needs business logic, survives configuration change and is cleared when the destination leaves. A plain class state holder, created with remember in Compose, holds UI logic and UI-element state that depends on UI-scoped things like focus, scroll, Resources or the NavController, and is reusable across screens. Longer-lived holders may be passed data into shorter-lived ones, never the other way round.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Official guidance: produce state in the holder closest to where it is consumed; plain class holders for UI logic and reusable widgets, ViewModel for business logic holders.
  • A plain holder dies with the composition and any needed persistence delegates to rememberSaveable (as rememberLazyListState does).
  • Dependency rule: a state holder can depend on others of equal or shorter lifetime. A UI holder should receive only the values it needs from the ViewModel, not the ViewModel itself.
  • ViewModel to plain holder: pass state and lambdas as parameters. Plain holder to ViewModel: do not.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Stable
class SearchBarState(
    private val focusRequester: FocusRequester,
    private val onSearch: (String) -> Unit,
) {
    var text by mutableStateOf("")
    fun submit() { if (text.isNotBlank()) onSearch(text.trim()) }
}

@Composable
fun rememberSearchBarState(onSearch: (String) -> Unit): SearchBarState {
    val focus = remember { FocusRequester() }
    return remember(onSearch) { SearchBarState(focus, onSearch) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating a ViewModel for a reusable chip group or search bar.
  • Passing a ViewModel to a plain holder, creating a lifetime-inversion dependency.
  • Forgetting rememberSaveable so UI state resets on rotation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does text-field state belong? → It depends on whether business logic needs it each keystroke; otherwise UI holder with saveable.
  2. Can a plain holder be tested? → Yes, as a JVM class if it avoids Android types.
  3. How do you share logic across screens? → Data/domain layer components, not ViewModel to ViewModel.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: ViewModel for everything. Senior assigns by lifetime and logic type and calls out the dependency direction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A design-system chip group used a ViewModel, which broke in dialogs and previews; moving to a state holder fixed both.

questions.promptHtml: Why should ViewModels avoid Android framework types, and how do you handle strings, permissions and navigation without them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It exposes whether a candidate can keep logic testable and leak-free.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A ViewModel outlives the Activity, so holding a Context, View or Fragment leaks. Beyond leaks, Android types force instrumented or Robolectric tests. I keep the ViewModel to plain Kotlin and expose data, with the UI resolving strings, launching permission requests and performing navigation. If I need a resource, I emit a UiText model or an ID.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Allowed exceptions: Application context via AndroidViewModel or APPLICATION_KEY, or an injected abstraction (StringProvider, Clock, ConnectivityMonitor) with a fake in tests. Prefer the abstraction.
  • Strings: emit UiText.Resource(R.string.x, args) or a raw string, resolved in the composable with stringResource. Localized strings depend on configuration, which is UI lifecycle-dependent per the official doc.
  • Permissions and activity results: UI layer owns the launcher; the ViewModel receives the outcome as an event/action.
  • Navigation: expose an intent such as onItemSelected(id) and let the UI navigate (event delivery detail in chunk 03).
  • Parcelable/Bundle types in SavedStateHandle are the pragmatic exception.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UiText {
    data class Res(@StringRes val id: Int, val args: List<Any> = emptyList()) : UiText
    data class Plain(val value: String) : UiText
}
@Composable fun UiText.asString(): String = when (this) {
    is UiText.Res -> stringResource(id, *args.toTypedArray())
    is UiText.Plain -> value
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• AndroidViewModel used to call getString in logic, locking out JVM tests and ignoring locale changes (the cached string is stale after a language switch).
  • Holding a Context obtained from an Activity.
  • Calling startActivity from the ViewModel via a stored reference.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Application context safe to hold? → Process lifetime, no Activity leak, but themes/locale are not Activity-specific.
  2. How do you show a runtime-localized error? → UiText resolved at render time.
  3. How would you enforce it? → Konsist/lint check on imports in ViewModel classes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "don't hold Context". Senior explains test cost, locale staleness and the allowed abstraction patterns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cached getString result displayed English after users switched locale within the app until the screen was recreated.

questions.promptHtml: Where should a ViewModel start its loading work: init, a load() call from the UI, or lazily when the state is first collected? What are the trade-offs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes lifecycle-aware thinking: duplicate loads, wasted work, and state that survives rotation but not a stale cache.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I prefer deriving state in a cold pipeline with stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)), so work starts when the UI collects and stops five seconds after it leaves, which spans rotation. Work in init runs once per ViewModel instance regardless of whether anyone is looking and is the simplest but wasteful and hard to retry. A UI-triggered load() risks being called on every recomposition or resume unless guarded.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Approach                    Starts when             Stops when              Retry/refresh        Risk
--------------------------  ----------------------  ----------------------  -------------------  ------------------------
init { launch { load() } }  ViewModel constructed   completes / VM cleared  needs explicit fn    runs with no UI; init-order bugs
UI calls load() on enter    UI decides              completes               explicit             double-calls on recreation
stateIn(Lazily)             first subscriber        never until VM cleared  none                 keeps upstream hot forever
stateIn(WhileSubscribed)    first subscriber        5s after last subscriber re-subscribes restarts  re-runs upstream after timeout
  • The 5 000 ms figure comes from the official guidance: it outlasts the Activity recreation gap in a rotation so upstream is not restarted, but still stops work when the app is backgrounded for longer (ANR-timeout-inspired; the docs describe it as covering configuration changes).
  • When the upstream restarts after the timeout, a cold flow re-executes, e.g. a fresh network call. Hence a repository with a cache or a Flow from Room is the natural source.
  • init and constructor order: property initializers run in declaration order; a launch in init that touches a property declared below sees null/default (and Main.immediate runs the first part synchronously).
  • Initial values: stateIn needs one; model Loading explicitly rather than an empty list that looks like "no data".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedViewModel(repo: FeedRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val uiState: StateFlow<FeedUiState> = repo.observeFeed()          // Room-backed Flow
        .map<List<Post>, FeedUiState> { FeedUiState.Success(it) }
        .catch { emit(FeedUiState.Error(it.message)) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), FeedUiState.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• init { launch { ... } } that mutates a MutableStateFlow declared lower in the class.
  • Calling vm.load() in LaunchedEffect(Unit) and also in init.
  • SharingStarted.Eagerly for expensive upstreams.
  • Forgetting a Loading initial state so the screen flashes empty.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens at the 5s boundary on a 6s backgrounding? → Upstream cancels; resubscribing restarts the flow collection.
  2. How do you do a manual refresh with this? → Combine a refresh trigger (MutableSharedFlow/Channel) via flatMapLatest, or call repo.refresh() separately.
  3. How do you run init work in tests? → Same dispatcher rules; with WhileSubscribed, you must collect in the test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE puts work in init. Senior chooses start/stop semantics deliberately and handles initial state, restarts and refresh.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed screen reloaded on every return from background longer than 5s, doubling API calls (about 30% extra QPS); a Room-backed source turned restarts into cache reads.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (1.1M DAU) has a restaurant list ViewModel. The API gateway shows GET /restaurants at about 2.7x the expected rate since release 5.12. Users report occasional list flicker (spinner, list, spinner). The code:

class RestaurantsViewModel(private val repo: RestaurantsRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState(loading = true))
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

    init { load() }

    fun load() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
            _state.update { it.copy(loading = false, items = repo.fetch()) }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun RestaurantsRoute(vm: RestaurantsViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.load() }
    val s by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    RestaurantsScreen(s)
}

Retrofit's average payload is 120 KB; p95 latency is 900 ms.
questions.promptHtml: What are the bugs and how do you fix them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove one of the calls." That misses overlapping jobs, no cancellation of the previous fetch, and rotation/background re-triggering.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did 5.12 add the LaunchedEffect? Is the route re-entered often (tabs, back stack)? Does rotation re-trigger? Does the repo dedupe in-flight calls? Error handling and result ordering?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the redundant LaunchedEffect load (server flag not needed) and ship; rollout staged at 10% watching QPS.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two loads at start: init plus LaunchedEffect; (b) LaunchedEffect(Unit) re-runs when the composable leaves and re-enters composition (tab switch, nav) and after rotation, as the effect is bound to composition, not the ViewModel; (c) overlapping loads racing so an older response overwrites a newer one; (d) CDN/API client retries (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: OkHttp logging interceptor or Charles; count requests per screen open; log vm.hashCode() at load; Compose recomposition/effect logs; a test counting fetch() calls after rotation.
  5. Root cause: Load is triggered from two places and nothing guards against re-entry or cancels the previous job, so every composition entry re-fetches while the spinner state flips, creating the flicker.
  6. Fix: Short-term: delete the LaunchedEffect and cancel the previous job. Long-term: make loading a pure function of subscription and an explicit refresh trigger.
class RestaurantsViewModel(repo: RestaurantsRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val refresh = MutableSharedFlow<Unit>(replay = 1).apply { tryEmit(Unit) }
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = refresh
        .flatMapLatest { flow { emit(UiState(loading = true)); emit(UiState(items = repo.fetch())) } }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState(loading = true))
    fun refresh() { refresh.tryEmit(Unit) }
}
  1. Prevention: Test asserting exactly one fetch per screen entry and after rotation; request-count dashboard per endpoint per session; review rule "load triggers live in one place".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not adding a boolean if (loading) return guard (it hides the cause and loses refresh); not moving to Eagerly. WhileSubscribed means a restart after 5s does refetch, so I'd pair it with a repo cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if product wants refresh on resume only after 5 minutes? → Track last-fetched timestamp in the repository, not the composable.
  • Does this change if the VM is activity-scoped? → The VM survives longer, but a LaunchedEffect would still fire per composition.
  • Why does the flicker appear? → Loading set true on each reload before data arrives.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team scaled the backend for a "traffic spike" that was just a LaunchedEffect(Unit) inside a tab screen; the bill dropped 25% after deleting four lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes one call and stops.
  • Hire: identifies double triggering plus lack of cancellation and fixes with reactive start.
  • Strong hire: adds request-count tests, explains WhileSubscribed restarts, and moves freshness policy to the data layer.

questions.promptHtml: How do you create a ViewModel that needs a runtime parameter (like a user ID or a list item ID) plus injected dependencies?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real screens take arguments; this checks you know the options and which survives recreation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: First choice: read the argument from SavedStateHandle (nav arguments land there), so it survives recreation and process death and needs no factory. If the value is not in nav args, use Hilt assisted injection: @AssistedInject on the ViewModel with an @AssistedFactory, @HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ...), and hiltViewModel(creationCallback = ...). Without Hilt, a viewModelFactory with custom CreationExtras.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• SavedStateHandle route: type-safe Navigation 2.8+ gives handle.toRoute<DetailRoute>(). Hilt's SavedStateHandle injection works with no extra code.
  • Assisted route: Hilt 2.49+ supports @HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = X.Factory::class); you supply the factory through creationCallback (verify the minimum Hilt version for your project). The runtime parameter is created for a particular ViewModel instance and is part of that instance's identity only through the key you give.
  • Gotcha: the ViewModel is cached under its key; navigating to a second detail with a different parameter and same default key returns the first VM. Use a distinct key or one VM per nav entry.
  • Without Hilt, custom CreationExtras.Key passed to viewModel(factory, extras).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ChatViewModel.Factory::class)
class ChatViewModel @AssistedInject constructor(
    private val repo: ChatRepo,
    @Assisted private val chatId: String,
) : ViewModel() {
    @AssistedFactory interface Factory { fun create(chatId: String): ChatViewModel }
}

@Composable
fun ChatRoute(chatId: String) {
    val vm = hiltViewModel<ChatViewModel, ChatViewModel.Factory>(
        key = chatId,
        creationCallback = { f -> f.create(chatId) },
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assisted parameters that are not restored after process death (they come from the composable caller, so the caller must restore them).
  • Missing key leading to a stale instance.
  • Using assisted when a nav argument would do.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why prefer SavedStateHandle? → Survives process death automatically.
  2. Who owns the key? → You, when reusing one owner for many instances.
  3. How do you test it? → Construct the ViewModel directly with fakes and the parameter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes a factory by hand. Senior picks the handle first, knows the assisted cache-key trap, and handles process death.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tablet master-detail screen reused one assisted ViewModel for every selected row until each detail got its own key.

questions.promptHtml: When would you scope a ViewModel to a navigation graph or a back stack entry, and what are the lifecycle pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flow-scoped state (onboarding, checkout) is common and error-prone.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Entry scope is the default and right for one screen. Graph scope is right for a multi-step flow whose steps share a draft, because the graph's entry stays on the back stack until the flow ends. The ViewModel lives until that entry is popped, so I must end the flow explicitly and avoid sharing too much mutable state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Get it with hiltViewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry(Route)) (or viewModel(parentEntry)), inside remember(entry) to avoid exceptions when the entry is not yet available during transitions.
  • Pitfalls: (1) getBackStackEntry throws IllegalArgumentException if the route is not on the back stack, which happens during pop animations; (2) saveState/restoreState keeps stores alive (see the checkout scenario); (3) process death restores the graph but the ViewModel is new, so only SavedStateHandle survives.
  • Prefer passing results forward by ID and persisting drafts rather than long-lived shared VM state.
  • Alternative: a flow-level state holder in the data layer scoped by a session ID.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
composable<Step2> { entry ->
    val parent = remember(entry) { navController.getBackStackEntry<OnboardingGraph>() }
    val vm: OnboardingViewModel = hiltViewModel(parent)
    Step2Screen(vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle().value, vm::onNext)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Accessing the parent entry without remember(entry) and crashing during navigation transitions.
  • Never popping the graph, so the VM and draft linger.
  • Using the graph VM for state that only one step needs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is the VM cleared? → When the graph entry is popped (no saveState).
  2. How do two siblings share data? → Common parent scope or a shared repository.
  3. How do you avoid graph-scope as a global store? → Keep it to flow drafts; persist results.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "scope to the graph". Senior covers the crash, saveState retention and the process-death gap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A signup flow crashed on back press with "No destination with route on back stack" until the parent lookup was wrapped in remember(entry).

questions.contextHtml:
A music app (3M DAU) added an Activity-scoped PlayerViewModel so a mini-player and the full player share state. After release 8.3, ANR rate rose from 0.25% to 0.55% and "Out of memory" crashes from 0.3% to 0.9% on 2-3 GB devices, mostly after 40+ minutes of use. A heap dump shows 38 instances of AlbumScreenState and a growing ArrayList<Listener> inside PlayerViewModel (11 000 entries). The ViewModel has:

fun registerProgressListener(l: ProgressListener) { listeners += l }

Each album screen registers in DisposableEffect but a code path skips onDispose removal for the "preview" button.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and say how you'd stop this class of issue.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the ViewModel smaller" or "call System.gc". Neither addresses the unbounded registry on a long-lived owner.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens register? Is the ViewModel Activity-scoped (so never cleared while the app is open)? Is the growth linear in navigation count? Did ANR growth correlate with GC pauses? Any background threads iterating the list?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side flag to disable the preview feature; hotfix that clears listeners when the registering screen's lifecycle ends.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) listener registry leak on a long-lived VM; (b) the listeners capture composable state (explains the 38 AlbumScreenState instances); (c) progress emissions on main iterating 11k listeners cause the ANRs; (d) image cache (red herring if heap dump points to listeners).
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump retained-size by class; LeakCanary; Android Studio allocation profiler; Perfetto trace showing main thread time in the progress dispatch loop; ANR traces in Play Console.
  5. Root cause: Activity-scoped VM lives for the whole session; an imperative listener list with a missed removal grows unbounded and retains UI state. Progress dispatch is O(n) on main, so ANRs follow.
  6. Fix: Short-term: guarantee removal (try/finally, or DisposableEffect always paired), de-dupe. Long-term: replace the listener list with a StateFlow the UI collects lifecycle-aware; flows have no registry to leak.
class PlayerViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _progress = MutableStateFlow(0L)
    val progress: StateFlow<Long> = _progress.asStateFlow()
}
// UI: val p by vm.progress.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  1. Prevention: Ban imperative listener registries in ViewModels; LeakCanary on debug and a soak test navigating 100 screens; memory and ANR alerts per release with staged rollout gates.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use WeakReference lists (nondeterministic), and not shrink the scope: shared player state genuinely needs an Activity or app owner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the player state live in a ViewModel at all? → Playback is app-level; a service-backed or application-scoped holder survives Activity death better.
  • Progress ticks at 10 Hz: recompose cost? → Sample/derive to the UI's needs (A3).
  • How to find this faster next time? → Alert on retained-heap growth in soak tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A leak that took 40 minutes to show was found by replaying a 1-hour session script in CI with a heap-size assertion.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC or caches.
  • Hire: reads the heap dump, finds the registry, replaces with a flow.
  • Strong hire: ties ANR to main-thread O(n) dispatch, adds soak tests and questions the VM-vs-app-scope choice.

questions.contextHtml:
A notes app (600k DAU) uploads attachments from NoteViewModel. Support reports "attachment missing" in about 0.8% of notes, mostly when users tap Save then immediately press back. Code:

fun save() { viewModelScope.launch { api.upload(file) } }
override fun onCleared() { socket.close() }

Logs: JobCancellationException: ViewModelScope was cancelled right after onCleared. The upload takes about 2 s on 4G, p95 6 s.
questions.promptHtml: Why is data lost and how do you fix it, including the cleanup in onCleared?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use GlobalScope". That leaks, ignores retries and process death.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the upload user-visible (must complete)? Does it need to survive process death? Is there idempotency on the API? What does the UI promise?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the back button during save for 2 s as a stopgap while the fix is built.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) viewModelScope cancelled at onCleared; (b) process killed after leaving the screen; (c) network failure with no retry (red herring: logs show cancellation).
  4. How I'd verify each: The cancel log line, timing between back press and cancel, an instrumented test with immediate back after save.
  5. Root cause: Work whose lifetime is the user's intent was bound to the screen's lifetime. viewModelScope is cancelled when the owner finishes.
  6. Fix: Enqueue a WorkManager job (expedited or with network constraint and a unique key) for the upload; the ViewModel only schedules and observes. For short in-process work, an injected application-scoped CoroutineScope (SupervisorJob, injected dispatcher) is acceptable. Keep onCleared only for synchronous teardown; closeables can be registered with addCloseable (Lifecycle 2.5+).
fun save() = workManager.enqueueUniqueWork(
    "upload-$noteId", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
    OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>().setConstraints(netConstraint).build())
  1. Prevention: Rule: user-intent work never runs in viewModelScope; instrumented back-after-save test; metrics on upload success per save.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blocking onCleared (it runs on the main thread), not GlobalScope, not NonCancellable in viewModelScope as a blanket habit (it runs without owner and no retry).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can onCleared launch coroutines? → The scope is already cancelled; do synchronous cleanup only.
  • How would you show progress after the screen is gone? → Observe WorkInfo from the next screen or a notification.
  • What about idempotency? → Use a client-generated ID so retries do not duplicate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 1% data-loss bug sat in the backlog for months because the success metric counted "save tapped" instead of "upload completed".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: GlobalScope or delaying finish.
  • Hire: moves to WorkManager and explains cancellation.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency, observability and correct onCleared semantics.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-editing app (900k DAU) crashes at 0.7% of sessions when backgrounded, only on Android 9-11 devices with many layers. Crashlytics:

java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1,254,412 bytes
  at android.app.servertransaction.TransactionExecutor.executeCallbacks
Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException

The ViewModel stores handle["layers"] = layers (a List<Layer> of Parcelables with embedded Bitmap thumbnails) and handle["history"] = undoStack. A typical project has 25 layers at about 40 KB each.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this crash, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception." The crash happens in the system's save path, not in your code, and caught or not the state is lost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the largest saved payload? Which OS versions crash (the bug is older than the exception on newer versions)? Are other libraries saving state too (Fragments, rememberSaveable)? Is the crash on background or on navigation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove thumbnails and undo history from the handle via a remote flag / hotfix; keep only the project ID.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) combined Bundle exceeding the Binder transaction limit (about 1 MB shared by all transactions in the process, so the real budget is smaller); (b) a second big saver such as rememberSaveable of a large list; (c) a leak causing extra payload (red herring: the size is arithmetic).
  4. How I'd verify each: Math: 25 layers x 40 KB = 1.0 MB for layers alone, plus history. Log Parcel.dataSize for the saved Bundle in debug; the TooLargeTool library or a debug dump of onSaveInstanceState sizes.
  5. Root cause: SavedStateHandle writes into the Activity's saved Bundle, which is sent to the system server through Binder when the Activity stops. Over the transaction limit it fails.
  6. Fix: Persist the project to disk (Room/files) as it changes, keep only projectId and a small cursor in the handle, and rebuild layers on restore.
class EditorViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle, private val projects: ProjectRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val projectId: String = handle["projectId"]!!
    val project = projects.observe(projectId)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}
  1. Prevention: Rule: SavedStateHandle holds IDs and small inputs only; a debug-build check that logs Bundle size when above 50 KB; process-death test.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not compressing into the Bundle (still limited and slow), not splitting across multiple keys (same transaction).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did Android 14 not crash? → Newer versions are more tolerant; behavior varies by OS (verify), do not rely on it.
  • Autosave frequency? → Debounced writes, not on every stroke.
  • Where do undo stacks belong? → Disk or recomputed state, never the Bundle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The crash only appeared in a beta of power users with huge projects, so staged rollout with crash gating caught it before the full release.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps in try/catch.
  • Hire: explains the Binder limit and moves data to disk with an ID.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the payload, adds size instrumentation and tests restoration.

questions.promptHtml: How do navigation arguments reach a ViewModel, what should you pass, and what happens on process death?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Argument passing is the classic source of stale-object and crash-after-restore bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Arguments are written into the entry's arguments Bundle and surfaced in the ViewModel's SavedStateHandle. With Navigation 2.8 type-safe routes I read them with handle.toRoute<Route>(). I pass identifiers and small primitives, not objects; the ViewModel loads data from the repository using the ID. Because arguments persist in the saved nav state, the ViewModel restores correctly after process death.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Flow: navigate(DetailRoute(id)) serializes the route into arguments; on entry creation the SavedStateViewModelFactory (or Hilt's) builds the handle seeded with those arguments (via DEFAULT_ARGS_KEY in CreationExtras).
  • Why IDs: objects can be stale, large and non-restorable; ID plus repository gives one source of truth.
  • Process death: the NavController restores the back stack with arguments; the new ViewModel gets them again. Anything passed via a shared in-memory holder (e.g. "set object in a singleton, then navigate") is gone.
  • Complex arguments: Nav 2.8 supports @Serializable types with custom NavType; keep them small (verify limits for your version).
  • Mutating arguments: handle entries are writable but the original arguments are not re-sent.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Serializable data class DetailRoute(val productId: String)

@HiltViewModel
class DetailViewModel @Inject constructor(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: ProductRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val productId = handle.toRoute<DetailRoute>().productId
    val state = repo.observe(productId)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing a whole product object (stale price after back navigation).
  • Using a static field to hand an object between screens (null after process death).
  • Reading the argument in the composable and passing it into the VM manually, bypassing the handle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the ID no longer exists after restore? → Model NotFound state in UiState.
  2. Why not pass the object for an instant UI? → Pass a minimal preview (title, image) if needed for transitions, but still load canonical data.
  3. How do you test it? → SavedStateHandle.toRoute in tests needs the route's serialization setup; for unit tests build the handle with the key map (verify exact test setup in your Nav version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE passes objects with Parcelable. Senior passes IDs and explains the restore path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "set current order in a singleton, then navigate" pattern crashed after process death on the payment screen for about 0.4% of sessions.

questions.contextHtml: You own a trading-style "Portfolio" screen on tablets and phones. It has four sections: holdings list (live prices, 150 rows), a performance chart, a news strip and an alerts banner. The current PortfolioViewModel is 1 400 lines, has 14 StateFlows and four coroutine pipelines, and a change to news logic caused a holdings regression last month. Team of 5, release every 2 weeks. A tablet layout shows all four at once; the phone shows tabs.
questions.promptHtml: One ViewModel or several? How would you split it, and what are the risks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "One ViewModel per section" without discussing cross-section state, or "keep one, it is simpler" without addressing the regression and size.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do sections share state (selected account, date range)? Do they load independently with independent errors? Is the phone tab UI created lazily? Who owns each section? What are the test pains?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would start by extracting pure logic (reducers/use cases) from the big ViewModel to shrink risk without changing scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) sections are independently refreshable, so separate state holders match the domain; (b) shared selection (account, range) is the real coupling; (c) one ViewModel is fine if split internally into collaborators; (d) performance (red herring: ViewModel count rarely matters, 4 objects are cheap).
  4. How I'd verify each: Draw the dependency graph of state; count shared inputs; check which flows depend on which; examine the git history for conflicts and regressions by section.
  5. Root cause: Section-independent work lives in one state holder, so change scope is unclear and tests need huge fixtures. The official guidance says screen-level state holders should not depend on one another, so sibling ViewModels reading each other is not the answer.
  6. Fix: Keep one screen-level ViewModel owning shared inputs (selected account, range) and exposing the combined route state; extract per-section logic into plain collaborators or use cases (HoldingsPipeline, NewsPipeline) that take the shared input flow as a parameter and return a Flow. Where a section is truly independent (news strip reused elsewhere), give it its own ViewModel with a key, fed shared inputs through arguments, not other ViewModels.
class PortfolioViewModel(account: AccountSelection, holdings: ObserveHoldings, news: ObserveNews) : ViewModel() {
    val ui = combine(holdings(account.selected), news(account.selected)) { h, n -> PortfolioUi(h, n) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), PortfolioUi.Loading)
}
  1. Prevention: Size guardrails in review, tests per pipeline, one owner per section.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No ViewModel-to-ViewModel dependency; no shared mutable singleton for section state; do not split purely by line count. A combined UiState re-renders all sections on one change, so with Compose I'd keep sections as separate stable state objects (A3).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Section errors must be independent? → Each pipeline exposes its own state with its own error; combine does not fail the others.
  • Tablet vs phone? → Same ViewModel serves both; layout differs in the UI.
  • Section reused on another screen? → Becomes its own ViewModel or a domain-level use case.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team split by screen region into four VMs that all read each other; extracting pure use cases instead cut test setup by two thirds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-in-one or one-per-pixel without reasoning.
  • Hire: separates shared inputs from section logic and extracts collaborators.
  • Strong hire: cites the no-sibling-dependency guidance, handles independent errors, and weighs Compose recomposition scope.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test a ViewModel that uses viewModelScope, StateFlow and a repository?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Test quality is a senior marker; most flaky ViewModel tests come from dispatcher misuse.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use a JVM unit test with a fake repository, replace Dispatchers.Main with a test dispatcher through a rule, run in runTest, and assert on the StateFlow, using Turbine for sequences. For stateIn(WhileSubscribed), I must collect in the test or the upstream never starts. I construct the ViewModel directly with SavedStateHandle(mapOf(...)) and inject dispatchers rather than hardcode them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate, which is unavailable on JVM; Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) fixes it. Reset in teardown.
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher runs eagerly (easy asserts, may hide ordering); StandardTestDispatcher queues until advanceUntilIdle/runCurrent (closer to production, more explicit).
  • stateIn(WhileSubscribed): start a collector, e.g. backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { vm.state.collect {} }.
  • Prefer fakes (an in-memory repo you can drive) over mocks; they test behavior, not call sequences.
  • Inject CoroutineDispatcher for withContext blocks so tests control time.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainDispatcherRule(val d: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(d)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}

class SearchVmTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule()

    @Test fun `query triggers results`() = runTest {
        val repo = FakeSearchRepo(listOf("kotlin"))
        val vm = SearchViewModel(SavedStateHandle(), repo)
        vm.state.test {                       // Turbine
            assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem())
            vm.onQuery("kot")
            assertEquals(Success(listOf("kotlin")), awaitItem())
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting resetMain, so tests leak into each other.
  • Asserting vm.state.value without any collector for a WhileSubscribed flow.
  • Mocking the repository and verifying call order.
  • Using delay with real time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why UnconfinedTestDispatcher vs Standard? → Eager vs explicit scheduling; start with Standard for correctness tests.
  2. How do you test a retry with backoff? → Virtual time with advanceTimeBy.
  3. How do you test process-death restore? → Build a new VM with a handle copied from the old one's keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE mocks and sleeps. Senior controls time, injects dispatchers and tests behavior through fakes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A suite's flakiness dropped from 8% to under 1% after replacing real delays and a shared Dispatchers.Main setup with a rule and virtual time.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech team (40 engineers) has a CI with 2 800 unit tests; 35 fail intermittently, about 6% of runs go red and each re-run costs 11 minutes of 12 parallel runners. The recurring failures are ViewModel tests:

kotlinx.coroutines.test.UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 10s, the test coroutine is not completing
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize
AssertionFailedError: expected:<Success> but was:<Loading>

Tests mix Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher()) inline, Thread.sleep(100), and GlobalScope.launch in a repository fake.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, fixes, and how the team prevents regressions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries to CI." This hides the flakiness and adds cost and false trust.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do failures cluster by module or by runner load? Are tests sharing static state? Which dispatcher do production classes hardcode? Is there a single test base?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the 35 tests into a non-blocking suite with owners and deadlines while fixes land; do not auto-retry silently.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Main dispatcher not set or not reset, leaking across tests; (b) code under test uses real dispatchers (withContext(Dispatchers.IO), GlobalScope) so work escapes virtual time; (c) collecting WhileSubscribed state without a subscriber ("Loading" forever); (d) CI machine load (red herring: virtual time removes timing dependence).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the failing class in isolation vs in the suite (order dependence); Gradle --tests with random ordering; grep for GlobalScope, Thread.sleep, Dispatchers.IO in the code under test; a stress job running a failing test 200 times.
  5. Root cause: Time and threads were real in places and virtual in others. The test scheduler cannot advance work scheduled on other dispatchers, and unreset Main leaks state across tests.
  6. Fix: Common MainDispatcherRule; inject dispatchers via an interface into repos and ViewModels; remove GlobalScope; collect with backgroundScope for WhileSubscribed; use fakes; replace sleeps with advanceUntilIdle/Turbine awaits.
interface DispatcherProvider { val io: CoroutineDispatcher; val default: CoroutineDispatcher }
class TestDispatchers(s: TestCoroutineScheduler) : DispatcherProvider {
    override val io = StandardTestDispatcher(s); override val default = StandardTestDispatcher(s)
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/Konsist ban on GlobalScope and hardcoded Dispatchers in production classes; flaky-test dashboard with owners; a repeat-run nightly job; a test template.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No blanket retries; no global UnconfinedTestDispatcher everywhere to make failures vanish (it hides ordering bugs); injecting dispatchers costs a little boilerplate but pays for itself.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about tests that need real concurrency? → A few dedicated integration tests on a real dispatcher with timeouts.
  • How do you measure success? → Flake rate and re-run minutes per week.
  • Hilt tests? → Replace the DispatcherProvider via a test module (see A4 Hilt chunk).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Quarantine with deadlines fixed 30 tests in two weeks; a no-retry policy forced the real fixes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds retries or sleeps.
  • Hire: standardizes the Main rule, dispatcher injection and fakes.
  • Strong hire: adds structural prevention (lint rules), metrics and a quarantine process.

questions.promptHtml: What logic belongs in a ViewModel versus use cases, repositories, and UI state holders? How do you stop a ViewModel from becoming a god object?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It evaluates judgment about boundaries and refactoring, not API knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The ViewModel's job is to turn user actions and data-layer streams into screen UI state, and to delegate business rules. Product rules and data access go to use cases and repositories; UI logic that needs Android/UI types goes to plain state holders in the UI. I watch for size, number of dependencies, unrelated state groups and logic that would be needed by another screen.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
UI (composables)        -> rendering, UI-element state, navigation calls, permission launchers
UI state holder (plain) -> UI logic needing UI-scoped types (focus, scroll, windowSizeClass)
ViewModel               -> screen state production, event handling, calling domain/data
Use case (optional)     -> reusable/complex business rule across screens
Repository / data       -> data access, caching, mapping
  • Official guidance: the ViewModel delegates business logic to domain/data layers; reusable logic across destinations belongs in a data- or domain-scoped component, not another ViewModel. Domain layer is optional.
  • God-ViewModel signals: more than about 6-7 constructor dependencies, 500+ lines, state fields that change independently, tests needing huge fixtures, and merge conflicts concentrated in one file. Treat those as heuristics, not rules.
  • Extraction order: (1) pure functions and mappers, (2) use cases for reused or complex rules, (3) split independent sections into their own state holders, (4) only then sibling ViewModels.
  • Avoid ViewModel-to-ViewModel calls and using a ViewModel as an event bus between screens.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CheckoutViewModel(
    private val placeOrder: PlaceOrderUseCase,   // rule lives here
    private val cart: CartRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    val ui = cart.observe().map(::toUi).stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), CheckoutUi.Loading)
    fun onPay() = viewModelScope.launch { placeOrder(cart.current()) } // delegate, no pricing math here
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pricing, validation and mapping logic embedded in the ViewModel and copy-pasted to a second screen.
  • Creating a use case per repository method with no logic (pure boilerplate).
  • Splitting into many ViewModels that read each other, increasing coupling.
  • Using the ViewModel for animations and scroll positions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a use case not worth it? → When it is a one-line pass-through with a single caller.
  2. How do you refactor without a rewrite? → Extract pure functions behind existing tests, then collaborators, keep the public state API stable.
  3. How do you measure it works? → Smaller diffs per feature, faster ViewModel tests, fewer cross-section regressions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel holds business logic". Senior: "ViewModel produces state and delegates; rules live in domain/data; UI logic stays UI", with measurable smell tests and an incremental refactor plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 2 000-line ViewModel duplicated discount rules also in the cart screen, so two screens showed different totals until the rule moved into one use case.
